thread.title: The High Yield Is Poison At GameStop - GameStop Corp. (NYSE:GME)

author: Julian Lin
title: The High Yield Is Poison At GameStop - GameStop Corp. (NYSE:GME)
text:
Thesis While the valuation at GameStop ( GME ) does indeed look compelling based on current financials, all of their core business segments are under extreme pressure from both e-commerce and brick & mortar competitors, the most significant being Amazon ( AMZN ). There is very real risk that financials see a sudden downturn as consumers quickly begin to shop elsewhere. This has not yet manifested itself in the past financials, but should investors really wait for the great awakening? I do not believe that the current 11.7% yield is enough to compensate for these risks as the apparent dividend coverage is only as stable as the potentially unstable future cash flows.
Business Overview GME operates 7,535 stores with the majority being in their core video game business:
( 2017 10-K )
In addition to selling both new and pre-owned games, they also are a reseller of Apple ( AAPL ) products and operate AT&T ( T ) branded stores through Spring Mobile.
( Spring Mobile )
The struggling financials As with many retailers, the rise of e-commerce has made competition fiercely intense as the average consumer is now more likely to compare prices with competitors. This has led many retailers including GME to rely on heavy promotions to keep customers coming through the door.
This means that while revenues have been strong the past year:
(2017 10-K)
We can see that for the majority of their segments, with the exception of Technology Brands, they saw deteriorating margins in 2017:
(2017 10-K)
In my view, they suffer from two important dangerous headwinds.
Free games are king Nowadays the top games that I frequently hear about, including League of Legends and most recently the smash-hit Fortnite, have begun a surprising trend of being free to play. Everyone likes free stuff, so it’s only natural that free high quality video games would be a popular phenomenon. The way these video game publishers make money thus would not be from purchase costs but instead from “micro transactions” which allow consumers to purchase add-ons to their games such as fancy outerwear or special music. The cost of these micro transactions could come anywhere between $0.99 and $99, or even more. It appears that the much lower price point of these transactions make the consumer more willing to shell out the cash and more often - the sum of all the tiny transactions may eventually add up to a much larger sum. This helps to explain why the free Facebook ( FB ) game Clash of Titans managed to help their creators pull in $2.3 billion in revenue in 2016. Why does this all matter to GME? This is a very powerful trend shaping how gamers will play and purchase games in the present and future. There may be a time where there is no need to go to GME to purchase games or even game consoles for that matter, and this is especially impactful considering how much a portion of revenues are coming from video games.
Digital is real In addition to the growing trend towards free games, there is also an arguably more powerful trend toward digital downloads versus disc purchases. Video game downloads obviously would not benefit GME as they would be essentially a removed middleman, and the appeal is quite clear. Digital downloads allow consumers to more quickly attain access to games at minimal effort - I call this part of the “new lazy society.” AMZN has a very strong offering of digital games including pre orders:
( Amazon )
GME used to be the preeminent store to preorder games with consumers often lining up for hours at the stores. This looks to be a thing of the past as video game companies have begun to realize that consumers want digital access.
This naturally will also greatly impact their pre-owned games segment because if gamers aren’t buying physical games, then they certainly have less of an inclination to buy pre-owned games.
Pre-owned games have historically been the profit producer for GME and in combination with video game hardware and software made up 50% of profits in 2017:
(2017 10-K)
The fact that their video game segments long term may go to zero should not be taken lightly to any investor or prospective investor.
Collectibles and Non Core operations GME has seen great results in their collectibles segment, with profits rising from $116.6 million in 2015 to $171.6 million in 2016 and then to $208.2 million in 2017. But is this sustainable? Should investors expect this to continue moving forward?
Past results don’t predict future performance. I believe this saying holds true here as collectibles in general are in a very crowded space as they not only are sold at more traditional stores like Target ( TGT ) or Walmart ( WMT ), but are also readily available online (again the impact of AMZN). I think the collectible performance will prove to be short lived as consumers are in my opinion more likely to acquire the product from competitors.
As for Spring Mobile and their Apple products, here too I am very skeptical. While I can see how Spring Mobile is useful in extending AT&T reach and penetration, I personally have made a point of taking all my business and issues directly to actual AT&T stores because I feel like they would be more knowledgeable and more equipped to handle my case. I feel like many people probably feel the same way. More importantly though, the telecom space is a very competitive environment with continued pricing pressure - AT&T is having a hard enough time generating growth or even maintaining a high amount of revenues. Wouldn’t Spring Mobile face even greater pressures considering that a certain cut must go back to AT&T? Still, this is very anecdotal and for sure their technology brands should perform much stronger than their video game segment. But at only 20% of profits, is it enough? Further, should investors really be counting on the non-core businesses to save the day?
Valuation and Dividends When thinking about the valuation, we must take the above issues into consideration. Might future results look even worse than past results as the trend accelerates? I certainly can not think of any catalyst that would slow down let alone reverse the trend.
I bet many readers are attracted to GME due to its $1.52 payout or 11.7% yield. I have also seen it written that GME should buy back its shares and that doing so would create significant value. I am skeptical.
While the 11.7% yield is adequately supported for the time being by $3.87 in normalized earnings, these earnings have been falling rapidly, as we can see cash flow from operations has fallen off the cliff from $656.8 million in 2015 to $537.1 million in 2016 and $434.9 million in 2017. If GME were to continue this deterioration of 18%, it’s clear to see that the 30% earnings yield isn’t enough (using a conservative 10% discount rate).
The question now is, will the earnings deterioration come to an end? As we can see below, their results have tended to be back loaded, thus we may not find out the bad news until later this year:
(2017 10-K)
As consumers become more and more used to the new types of games and the new ways to acquire the games, as well as collectibles and their Technology Brands, this looks like we may see a very disappointing a quarter quite soon which makes it clear that GME is facing secular headwinds. The only argument I could see for business to survive is that they have been doing ok in the last - and this is no argument in my book.
It looks to me like the great majority of their revenues comes from segments which are in the crosshairs of e-commerce and AMZN. That isn’t a great place to be, and I do not have the confidence to say that they will escape unscathed.
I find it easier to believe that in the long term all their core sources of revenue are a big zero and warn readers that the past steady revenues should not be extrapolated to hypothesize that earnings will continue to decline only steadily into the future.
The main thesis to purchase shares thus would be if the dividend adequately compensates for the risk of a dying business. In my opinion the 11.7% yield just doesn’t cut it in this respect - I need at least 20%, which would price GME at $7.60 per share.
Conclusion GME offers a high 11.7% yield which is hard to ignore, but once we look past the dividend, it becomes clear that the safety of the dividend is anything but clear. It would be a mistake to let the past stable performance sway you into thinking the future would be more of the same. The core businesses of GME are a long term zero and thus the current valuation just isn’t compelling.
